migrationNotes: Spine: a party organiser needs one list of everyone on the reply list or the badge list, and the same two-sided lookup is followed from RIGHT JOIN to FULL OUTER JOIN, the count of its rows, the NULLs that show who is missing, and a test in ON that creates more unmatched rows.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-preserve-either-side-8 (which join keeps both) and -9 (why Dee is not paired with order 107). Both are taught on the third screen.

lesson.title: Keep unmatched rows on either side

steps.headline: Left, right and the mirror image

lead.text: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the table written first. When the unmatched rows that matter are in the other table, you want the mirror image. That is RIGHT JOIN, which keeps every row of the table written second and puts NULL on the left wherever a row there has no partner.

The party lists show both. Ana replied but has no badge, so she has no partner in the badge list. Dot has a badge but never replied, so she has none in the reply list. Ben and Cy are on both lists. A LEFT JOIN from the replies to the badges keeps Ana. A RIGHT JOIN keeps Dot. Which one to use depends on whose missing partner you care about.

afterFigure.text: In the picture the first query starts from the replies and keeps all three guests, with Ana's badge blank. The second keeps all three badges, with Dot's reply blank. Each has three rows, and each drops one of the two unmatched people. Neither is wrong, because each answers a different question.

queries.label: Keep every reply
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g LEFT JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: Keep every badge
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g RIGHT JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY b.name;

lead.text: Make the combined list by hand, with a line for everyone who is on either list.

Sometimes neither side may lose anyone. The combined guest list needs Ana from one list and Dot from the other, along with the people on both. FULL OUTER JOIN does that. It returns every matched pair, then adds each unmatched row of the left table with NULLs on the right, and each unmatched row of the right table with NULLs on the left.

That gives a way to count the result. The number of rows is the number of matched pairs, plus the unmatched rows on the left, plus the unmatched rows on the right. An unmatched left row is never paired with an unmatched right row, because their keys differ, so each stays in a row of its own.

afterFigure.text: The first query in the picture is an inner join and returns two rows, for Ben and Cy. The second is the full join. It returns four: the two matches, Ana with a blank badge and Dot with a blank reply. Reading the NULLs shows who is missing from which list.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g INNER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: Keep both sides
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name);

lead.text: The shop's orders now include a guest order, 107, with no customer. Dee still has no order. Each join preserves one side.

reveal.text: You picked the side that RIGHT keeps: the table written on the right. Its unmatched row stays, and the other side's unmatched row is dropped.

queries.label: Preserve customers
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: The same two tables, with guest order 107 included. A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps the matched pairs and the unmatched rows from both sides.

reveal.text: You added the matches to the unmatched rows from each side. Both kinds of absence are rows of the result.

queries.label: Matches only
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c INNER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve both sides
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: With the guest order in the table, the shop has a customer with no order and an order with no customer. A LEFT JOIN from customers to orders keeps Dee and loses the guest order. A RIGHT JOIN keeps the guest order and loses Dee. Each returns seven rows: six matched pairs plus one kept row.

Equal counts do not mean equal results. Two joins can return the same number of rows while keeping different records, and only the NULLs show which side was kept. Look for the blanks in a result before you trust its size.

afterFigure.text: One more fact helps with counting. A RIGHT JOIN returns at least one row for every row of the right table, and exactly one when each of those rows matches no more than one row on the left. A right table of five rows that each match at most once gives five rows, wherever the matches fall.

queries.label: Preserve customers
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

queries.label: Preserve orders
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c RIGHT JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id, c.id;

lead.text: After a full join the NULLs say which side lacked a partner. If the guest column is NULL, the row is a badge with no reply. If the badge column is NULL, the row is a reply with no badge. Testing one side's key with IS NULL picks out the rows where that side was missing.
As in the last lesson, choose a key that is always filled on a real row, such as the name. A real row cannot have a NULL there, so a NULL always means that nothing matched.

afterFigure.text: The first query asks for the rows where the badge is NULL and finds Ana, who replied and has no badge. The second asks for the rows where the guest is NULL and finds Dot. A count of rows cannot tell the two apart, but the blanks can.

queries.label: Badge is NULL
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name WHERE b.name IS NULL ORDER BY g.name;

queries.label: Guest is NULL
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name WHERE g.name IS NULL ORDER BY b.name;

lead.text: The shop's customers and orders are joined again, with every unmatched row kept. Think about which side a NULL key points to.

reveal.text: You read the NULL key to see which side was absent. A row count alone cannot tell you that.

queries.label: First test
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.id;

queries.label: Second test
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

steps.headline: A test in the ON condition

lead.text: A condition in ON decides which rows can pair. In a full join a row that fails the condition is kept as an unmatched row on its own side, and so adding a test to ON can create more unmatched rows.

Suppose the badges have colours, and the rule is to pair a guest only with a blue badge. Ben's badge is blue, so Ben still pairs. Cy's badge is red, so the pair fails the rule. Cy the guest and Cy the badge are now two unmatched rows, one on each side.

afterFigure.text: The first query matches on name alone and returns four rows. The second adds the colour test and returns five: Ben's pair, then Ana and Cy as replies with no badge, then Cy and Dot as badges with no reply. The test removed nothing. It turned one matched row for Cy into two unmatched ones.

queries.label: Match on name
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name);

queries.label: Match on name and blue
queries.sql: SELECT g.name AS guest, b.name AS badge FROM guests AS g FULL OUTER JOIN badges AS b ON b.name = g.name AND b.colour = 'blue' ORDER BY COALESCE(g.name, b.name), b.name;

lead.text: The paid test now sits in the ON condition of the full join. Orders that fail it stay in the result as unmatched rows.

queries.label: Match every status
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

queries.label: Only paid matches
queries.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.status FROM customers AS c FULL OUTER JOIN orders AS o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid' WHERE c.id IS NULL ORDER BY o.id;

lesson.orientation: Compare RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN with a guest order that has no customer reference.
lesson.reviewLabel: Keep unmatched rows on either side
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A party organiser has two lists. The reply list has the guests who said they were coming: Ana, Ben and Cy. The badge list has the names that were printed on badges: Ben, Cy and Dot. The two lists mostly agree, but not entirely.

The organiser wants one list of everyone who appears on either. Ben and Cy are on both lists and go down once each. Ana replied but has no badge, so she goes down anyway. Dot has a badge but never replied, and she goes down too. Keeping only the names that appear on both lists would lose two people who matter.

The last lesson kept the customer with no orders. This one keeps unmatched rows from either side, so that nobody is lost from a list because the other list has no partner for them. It also covers what the blanks in the combined list tell you.

intro.promise: By the end you'll choose which side of a join to preserve, and read the NULLs that show who is missing.

recap.keyIdea: A RIGHT JOIN preserves the right table and a FULL OUTER JOIN preserves both. A NULL key shows which side had no match.

blocks.text: You combined two lists into 4 names, then counted 8 rows in the full join of the shop's tables. With the paid test in the ON condition, 3 order rows had no customer.

recap.nextHook: Joins settle which rows from two tables belong together. Some questions need an answer that the table itself has to supply first, such as a class average that decides who gets a sticker. The next lesson puts one query inside another to get it.

questions.prompt: Which unmatched row does customers RIGHT JOIN orders preserve?
hints: RIGHT preserves the right-hand orders table.

acceptedIdeas: Guest order 107, which has no customer reference
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A RIGHT JOIN preserves the orders side. Guest order 107 survives even though it has no matching customer; customer columns for that row are NULL.

choices.label: Guest order 107, which has no customer reference

questions.onCorrect: Guest order 107. RIGHT JOIN keeps every order, so the order with no customer stays.

misconceptions.feedback: Dee is a customer, and customers are the left-hand table. RIGHT keeps the other side.
RIGHT JOIN preserves the unmatched rows of one table.

questions.prompt: How many rows does the FULL OUTER JOIN return with the added guest order?
hints: Keep both kinds of unmatched row.
Do not pair Dee with the guest order; their keys do not match.
Add the six matching pairs and the two unmatched rows from opposite sides.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six matching pairs plus Dee's unmatched row plus the guest order make eight.

questions.onCorrect: 8. Six matched pairs, plus Dee and the guest order as unmatched rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the matches alone. Both unmatched rows are kept too.
That keeps one unmatched row. A FULL JOIN keeps both kinds.

questions.prompt: In the full join of customers and orders, which case does c.id IS NULL identify?
hints: Inspect the side named by the missing key.

acceptedIdeas: An order without a matched customer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: In the full join, a NULL customer id with an order present marks an order that did not match a customer. The full join preserves unmatched rows from both inputs.

choices.label: An order without a matched customer

questions.onCorrect: An order without a matched customer. c.id is NULL where no customer matched.

misconceptions.feedback: That is where o.id is NULL. Here the customer key is the NULL one.
The test is on the customer key, not on an amount.

questions.prompt: With the paid test in ON, how many unmatched order rows pass c.id IS NULL?
hints: A failed ON test does not remove a preserved order.
Count both pending orders and the guest order.
The unmatched order ids are 104, 106 and 107; count the records rather than their customer references.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Pending orders 104 and 106 do not match under that ON condition; guest order 107 also has no customer match.

questions.onCorrect: 3. A failed ON test keeps the order as an unmatched row, so both pending orders join the guest order.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the guest order. The failed ON test leaves the pending orders unmatched too.
That counts the pending orders alone. The guest order is unmatched as well.

questions.prompt: A contains ids 1, 2, 3. B contains ids 2, 4. Each id appears once. How many rows does A FULL JOIN B ON A.id = B.id return?
hints: Count the matching pair once.
Retain all three unmatched ids.
Keep every id from A, then add the id from B that is not already represented.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 2 matches; ids 1 and 3 remain from A; id 4 remains from B. Total: four.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Ids 1, 2, 3 and 4: the shared id appears once.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the id found only in B. FULL keeps both sides' unmatched rows.
The shared id appears once, not twice.

questions.prompt: Can two joins have the same row count but retain different records?
hints: LEFT and RIGHT each returned seven here, but their unmatched rows differ.

acceptedIdeas: Yes; compare which side is preserved
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Equal row counts do not establish equivalent joins. Inspect the retained records and the NULL-extended columns to see which side each join preserves.

choices.label: Yes; compare which side is preserved
No; equal counts prove equal results
Only when every key is duplicated

questions.onCorrect: Yes. Compare which side is preserved: the counts can agree while the records differ.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal counts say nothing about which rows were kept.
Duplicates are not needed. Different preserved sides can give equal counts.

questions.prompt: Guests who replied: Ana, Ben and Cy. Badges printed: Ben, Cy and Dot. You make one list of everyone who is on either list. How many different names are on it?
hints: Which names appear on both lists?
Each person should appear once.
Take everyone from the first list, then add anyone only on the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ana, Ben, Cy and Dot: Ben and Cy are on both lists but count once each.

questions.onCorrect: 4. A combined list keeps people from both sides, matched or not. A FULL join keeps rows in the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts Ben and Cy twice. Each person is one line.

questions.prompt: Which join keeps a customer with no orders and an order with no customer?
hints: Which join keeps unmatched rows from both tables?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both tables.

questions.onCorrect: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps matched pairs and unmatched rows from both tables.

misconceptions.feedback: LEFT keeps only the customers' side. The order with no customer would be lost.
INNER JOIN keeps matches only, so neither unmatched row stays.

questions.prompt: Why is Dee not paired with order 107?
hints: What does the ON condition compare?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Their keys do not match. Order 107 has no customer, and Dee has no order.

questions.onCorrect: A pair exists only when the ON condition is true. Dee and order 107 share no key.

choices.label: A customer and an order can never be paired.
FULL OUTER JOIN never pairs rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Customers and orders pair all the time, through the key.
It pairs every match first, then keeps the unmatched rows.

questions.prompt: A holds ids 1, 2 and 3. B holds ids 2, 4 and 5. Each id appears once. How many rows does A RIGHT JOIN B ON A.id = B.id return?
hints: Which table does RIGHT JOIN keep every row of?
Matched or not, each row of that table appears.
Count the ids in that table.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of B. B has three ids, and each appears once.

questions.onCorrect: 3. RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table, so its row count follows B.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a FULL JOIN. RIGHT keeps unmatched rows from B only.
RIGHT keeps every row of B, matched or not. Count B's ids.
